title_en: Trying to Save the World Is No Excuse
subtitle_zh: 本期节目讨论了针对中概券商看跌期权买家的内幕交易诉讼、Anthropic CEO 放慢前沿 AI 开发的备忘录所引发的反垄断争议，以及养老金与 401(k) 的回归。
description: Trying to Save the World Is No Excuse

turns.en: Bloomberg Audio Studios. Podcasts. Radio. News.
turns.zh: 彭博音频工作室（Bloomberg Audio Studios）。播客、广播、新闻。

turns.en: What are you reading, Matt Levine?
turns.zh: 你在读什么书，Matt Levine？

turns.en: You know, I'm reading Absalom, Absalom. It's a little much.
turns.zh: 这个嘛，我在读《押沙龙，押沙龙！》（Absalom, Absalom!）。有点难啃。

turns.en: Many people think that's one of the greatest novels to ever do it.
turns.zh: 很多人认为那是有史以来最伟大的小说之一。

turns.en: I know. I know.
turns.zh: 我知道，我知道。

turns.en: Did you read it because of the Dwight Garner review of The Disappearers that mentioned it as one of the best? You did.
turns.zh: 你读它，是不是因为 Dwight Garner 那篇《消失者》（The Disappearers）的书评里把它列为最佳之一？你就是。

turns.en: Well played. Wow. From downtown. This is like such not money stuff content. Yes. Sylvia accurately identified why I am reading Absalom, Absalom. It's like a little much, man. It's a little much. Okay.
turns.zh: 漂亮，服了。哇。这一记远投三分。这完全不是《Money Stuff》该有的内容啊。没错。Silvia 精准地说中了我在读《押沙龙，押沙龙！》的原因。它是有点难啃，老兄。真的有点难啃。好吧。

turns.en: Absalom, Absalom is your fiction. What's your non?
turns.zh: 《押沙龙，押沙龙！》算你的虚构类。那非虚构类呢？

turns.en: My usual division is fiction, nonfiction, and math or finance. But then also, I usually try to have two paper books going and one book on my phone so I can read it while walking the dog. And so right now, my phone book is also fiction. It's Colson Whitehead's Sag Harbor.
turns.zh: 我通常的分类是虚构类、非虚构类，以及数学或金融类。另外，我一般会同时读两本纸质书，再在手机里放一本，这样遛狗的时候也能看。所以现在手机里那本也是虚构类——是 Colson Whitehead 的《萨格港》（Sag Harbor）。

turns.en: What drove you to that? Wistful feelings about the end of the summer?
turns.zh: 是什么让你挑了它？是对夏天将尽的一丝怅惘？

turns.en: So yes. So well-identified, but no, there's a much more specific answer.
turns.zh: 算是吧。猜得真准，不过不对，还有个具体得多的答案。

turns.en: Give me one more.
turns.zh: 再给我一个。

turns.en: Which is that I was In Montauk, Reading the East Hampton Star, which featured a write-up of a book event that Colson Whitehead did at, I don't know, the East Hampton Public Library. Right, for the new one. And it was just a good, he sounds fun, and so I was like, I have late summer nostalgia, so I bought Sag Harbor from my phone. Hello, and welcome to the Money Slip Podcast. I'm Matt Levine. I wrote the Money Slip column for Bloomberg Opinion. I'm joined by.
turns.zh: 就是：我当时在蒙托克（Montauk），在读《东汉普顿星报》（East Hampton Star），上面有一篇报道，写 Colson Whitehead 在——我也不知道——东汉普顿公共图书馆办的一场活动，是为他新书办的。写得挺好，他听起来很有意思，于是我想，我这不是有夏末的怀旧情绪嘛，就在手机上买了《萨格港》。大家好，欢迎收听《Money Stuff》播客。我是 Matt Levine，《Money Stuff》专栏的作者，为彭博观点（Bloomberg Opinion）撰稿。今天与我搭档的是——

turns.en: I'm Sylvia Killingsworth. I edit the OnBooks newsletter.
turns.zh: 我是 Silvia Killingsworth，负责编辑《On Books》书评通讯。

turns.en: Sylvia is our returning guest co-host.
turns.zh: Silvia 是我们的回归客座联合主持。

turns.en: Had so much fun.
turns.zh: 上次玩得太开心了。

turns.en: The last time. So in May of this year, China announced a crackdown on basically cross-border trading from its brokerages. So some Chinese brokerage firms, their stocks dropped a lot because they got in trouble and they were restricted from doing some of the trades that had made them a lot of money. And just before that happened, people bought a lot of puts on several Chinese brokerage stocks. And Susquehanna International Group, which is a big options market maker, sold a lot of those puts. And they went to court in the US in June and said, people who are buying these puts, we have statistical data that makes it look really suspicious that they bought these puts. There's no news. They just bought a lot of very short-dated.
turns.zh: 上次合作很愉快。今年 5 月，中国宣布对券商的跨境交易展开整顿。一些中国券商因此惹上了麻烦，被限制做某些原本让它们赚得盆满钵满的交易，股价大跌。而就在这件事发生之前，有人大量买入了好几只中国券商股的看跌期权（puts）。Susquehanna International Group（SIG）是一家大型期权做市商，卖出了大量这些看跌期权。今年 6 月，他们到美国法院起诉，说：买这些看跌期权的人——我们有统计数据，显示他们买入的行为非常可疑。当时根本没有消息，他们却大量买入期限极短的期权。

turns.en: They must have known.
turns.zh: 他们肯定提前知道了。

turns.en: Because they paid off a lot of money.
turns.zh: 因为这些期权最后兑现了一大笔钱。

turns.en: Somehow.
turns.zh: 总归是用了什么法子知道的。

turns.en: They must have known. They must have been.
turns.zh: 他们肯定知道了。他们肯定是……

turns.en: Somebody must have leaked somewhere.
turns.zh: 肯定有人在什么地方泄了密。

turns.en: It guesses who they were. Right. Because like insider trading laws are weird. You need to have a fiduciary duty. That would be illegal. You need to be in breach of some duty to someone. And so they're like, they must have been either Chinese regulators or employees at these brokerage firms and had some duty to keep it confidential. And instead they traded on it. And so we want the money back. And they sued like 100 John Doe defendants. They don't know who they are.
turns.zh: 于是就得猜他们是谁了。对。因为内幕交易的法律很别扭：你得负有信义义务（fiduciary duty），那样才算违法；你得违背了对某人的某种义务。所以他们的说法是：这些人要么是中国监管者，要么是这些券商的员工，负有保密义务，却拿这消息去交易了。所以我们想把钱要回来。他们起诉了大约 100 名“无名氏”（John Doe）被告——因为他们不知道这些人是谁。

turns.en: 100 Johns Doe.
turns.zh: 100 个“无名氏”。

turns.en: Yeah. they're like customers of a couple of like Chinese brokerages. And I think of interactive brokers that you asked for. And they basically like went to court. First of all, you get the money back, but secondly to like immediately get an injunction to like freeze these accounts. Yep. And this month they lost the preliminary injunction. Basically the judge was like, Well, the case can go forward maybe, like, it's fine, but, like, we're not going to freeze all these accounts because he.
turns.zh: 对。这些人像是几家中国券商的客户——我记得其中一家是盈透证券（Interactive Brokers）。他们上法院，一是为了把钱要回来，二是为了立刻拿到禁令，冻结这些账户。是的。而这个月，他们在初步禁令这一步败诉了。基本上法官的意思是：嗯，案子也许可以继续审下去，那没问题，但我们不会冻结所有这些账户，因为他——

turns.en: Just didn't... It's impossible to know which one's who's what.
turns.zh: 他只是……根本没法知道哪个是哪个、谁是谁。

turns.en: He just didn't, like, entirely believe that they were all insider trading.
turns.zh: 他只是没法完全相信这 100 个人全都在搞内幕交易。

turns.en: All 100 of them are holding hands and insider trading together.
turns.zh: 100 个人手拉手一起做内幕交易。

turns.en: Right, right.
turns.zh: 对，对。

turns.en: So what was happening? If not all 100, some number of them, but the rest were kind of just following the pack.
turns.zh: 那当时到底发生了什么？如果不是全部 100 个，那也是其中一部分，剩下的人算是跟着起哄。

turns.en: Yeah, it's unclear, right? Like, there could be no insider trading. Like, I think, like, the circumstantial evidence is reasonable that maybe someone was insider trading.
turns.zh: 对，说不清楚。可能压根就没有内幕交易。我觉得，从间接证据看，说“也许有人在内幕交易”是合理的。

turns.en: But all 100 of them, eh. 100 is even kind of a fake number. Sure, but we're calling it 100.
turns.zh: 但整整 100 个？呃，100 这数字本身就有点假。——当然，但我们姑且就叫它 100。

turns.en: You just say John Does 1 through 100. Sure. But yeah, all 100 love them, let's say. We don't know. I've written about this before. If you get accused of insider trading and you are not a U.S. national and they freeze your account, it is probably not wise to get on a plane and fly to New York and say, I'd like my money back, because they might arrest you for doing the insider trading. But if you're totally innocent, you can take a shot. And so, in fact, a couple of– I don't know if they flew to New York. But a couple of the like John Doe's came to court.
turns.zh: 你就写“无名氏 1 到 100 号”呗。当然。好，那就假设 100 个全中吧。反正我们不知道。这事我以前写过：如果你被指控内幕交易，又不是美国公民，账户还被冻结了，那多半不明智的做法就是买张机票飞到纽约说“我要拿回我的钱”——因为他们可能以内幕交易的罪名把你抓了。但如果你完全清白，你可以赌一把。事实上，有几个——我不知道他们是不是飞来了纽约——但确实有几个“无名氏”出庭了。

turns.en: And used their real names.
turns.zh: 而且用了他们的真名。

turns.en: Yeah. And we're like, no, no, I'm not John Doe. I'm this guy. And here's why I bought these put options, right? And it's like, you know, I was on message boards and I saw people worrying about a potential crackdown. And I saw people buying put options and I thought, huh, that's weird. I saw volatility going up. And so like some of that, you know, it's always possible that that is like self-serving, right? And that like people are Sure. They can just say that. But to be fair, these people are not like, I'm a Chinese securities regulator, just coincidentally. It's like they're not Chinese securities regulators. Maybe they were tipped by insiders, but quite possibly their story is true and they saw someone else buying put options.
turns.zh: 对。他们说：不不不，我不是“无名氏”，我就是某某某，这是我买这些看跌期权的原因。理由大概是：你知道，我当时在论坛上看到有人担心可能会有一场整顿，又看到有人在买看跌期权，我心想“咦，奇怪”，还看到波动率在上升。这里面当然有可能是在自我开脱——人嘛，当然可以随便这么说。但公平地讲，这些人并不是“我碰巧是中国证券监管者”那种情况；他们不是中国证券监管者。也许他们是被内部人透了消息，但也很可能他们说的是真的——就是看到别人在买看跌期权。

turns.en: I was just doing what that guy was doing. I don't know why he was doing it, but I have a good guess.
turns.zh: “我只是照着那哥们儿在做。我不知道他为什么这么做，但我大概猜得到。”

turns.en: Right. And people email me about this sometimes. To some people, it feels wrong to buy options. Because you see a big options trade and you have a good guess about why. If you see, looking at public stock tapes, if you just see a public trade and you're like, that must be insider trading, and then you go trade on it, people are like, that's insider trading too, but I disagree. I think that is totally fine.
turns.zh: 对。时不时有人就此给我发邮件。对某些人来说，这样买期权感觉不对劲：因为你看到一笔大额的期权交易，又对原因有个八九不离十的猜测。如果你盯着公开的股票成交记录（tape），看到一笔公开交易，心想“那肯定是内幕交易”，然后跟着去交易，有人就会说“那也是内幕交易”。但我不同意。我觉得那完全没问题。

turns.en: So trading on what appears from the outside to be insider trading, you're saying is essentially still outsider.
turns.zh: 所以你的意思是：根据一个从外部看起来像内幕交易的行为去交易，本质上你仍然是个“局外人”（outsider）。

turns.en: Yeah. If you're trading on public information, that happens to be.
turns.zh: 对。如果你是根据公开信息在交易，只不过这信息恰好……

turns.en: The public information is I saw it in the tape.
turns.zh: 公开信息就是“我在成交记录里看到的”。

turns.en: And like, you know, if you know, like if like the CEO of the company calls you and like, hey, I'm going to do a big options trade because we're getting acquired. Then like, that's bad. Right. But if you just.
turns.zh: 你知道，如果是那家公司的 CEO 打电话给你说“嘿，我要做一笔大额期权交易，因为我们要被收购了”，那就不好了。对。但如果你只是——

turns.en: If you're looking at the shape of the trade.
turns.zh: 如果你只是看这笔交易的形态。

turns.en: If you just look at, if you're just a momentum trader, then you're fine.
turns.zh: 如果你只是看盘、只是个动量交易者（momentum trader），那你就没事。

turns.en: You're riding the wave.
turns.zh: 你是在顺浪而行。

turns.en: And so, you know, some, you know, between. one in 99 of these Susquehanna customers were probably doing that. And Susquehanna's point, which I think is fair, is we can't really tell who is who. Right.
turns.zh: 所以说，这些 Susquehanna 的客户里，99 个当中大概有一个是真这么干的。而 Susquehanna 的观点——我觉得站得住脚——就是：我们实在分不清谁是谁。对。

turns.en: And these people made money at our expense.
turns.zh: 而且这些人是拿我们的钱赚到了钱。

turns.en: Right. And the judge's point, which I think is also fair, is like, I didn't tell you to sue 100 John Does. Right. You sued the people who did it.
turns.zh: 对。而法官的观点——我觉得同样站得住脚——是：我又没让你们去起诉 100 个“无名氏”。你们应该去告真正干了这事的人。

turns.en: Right. Tell me, give me the evidence of them actually doing it and then we can talk.
turns.zh: 对。拿出他们真干了这事的证据给我，然后我们再谈。

turns.en: I do think that like, you know, maybe the case proceeds and they like, you know, subpoenaed the brokerages and they get some information and maybe they can.
turns.zh: 我确实觉得，案子也许会继续审下去，他们可以向券商发传票，拿到一些信息，也许能——

turns.en: What are they looking for? They're looking for like, oh, I texted my buddy from college and that's how I learned that, you know, they're looking for.
turns.zh: 他们在找什么？他们是在找那种“哦，我给大学哥儿们发了条短信，我就是这么知道的”——他们要找的是这类东西。

turns.en: Or just like literally the names of the accounts, right? Where like, if you like match the name with like the head of the Chinese securities regulator, like, oh, that guy might be insider trading, right? But yeah, I think it's very hard to like correlate a bunch of traders in a foreign country with like who you think might be insider trading. I think it's the sort of thing that a securities regulator can look into. And I think securities regulators might be looking into this, but it's very hard for Susquehanna.
turns.zh: 或者干脆就是账户的名字。如果你把名字和某个中国证券监管机构的头头对上号，“哦，那人可能在搞内幕交易”。但是啊，我觉得要把一个外国的一堆交易者，跟你认为可能在内幕交易的人对应起来，非常难。这种事更适合证券监管机构去查。我觉得监管机构可能确实在查，但对 Susquehanna 来说太难了。

turns.en: It's hard to identify the needle.
turns.zh: 大海捞针太难了。

turns.en: Yeah. It's hard to prove who insider traded and who didn't. And like they have, you know, they do the best they can with like statistical, like doesn't this trade look weird. Right.
turns.zh: 对。要证明谁搞了内幕交易、谁没搞，很难。他们只能尽力用统计手段，就是那种“这笔交易难道不奇怪吗”。对。

turns.en: But overall Susquehanna's case is like, but somebody did probably most likely. And don't you see that that's why we lost so much money. I mean, I know there are market makers that they have to, but like, Isn't there some point when you're selling those out-of-the-money put options where you're like, hmm, we're selling a lot of these. This is weird.
turns.zh: 但 Susquehanna 的整体主张就是：“可总归有人干了，八成就是有人干了。你难道不明白这就是我们亏这么多的原因吗？”我是说，我知道做市商有不得不做的义务，但难道在你卖那些价外（out-of-the-money）看跌期权的时候，就没有某一刻你会想“嗯，我们卖出去太多了，这不对劲”？

turns.en: So, one, I think I talked about this with Kate on this podcast. Ages ago, Jeff Yass, the founder of Susquehanna, did an interview with the Market Wizards series of books where he talks about this problem. In the 90s, getting picked off by selling a bunch of call options right before a merger. And then sometimes it was the insider traders who then gave the money back because the SEC came after them. And he's kind of like, yeah, but like we're a market, like it's our job.
turns.zh: 第一，我想我很久以前在这个播客里跟 Katie 聊过这事。Susquehanna 的创始人 Jeff Yass 在“市场奇才”（Market Wizards）系列书里做过一次访谈，谈到这个问题：上世纪 90 年代，在一起并购发生前卖出一大堆看涨期权（calls），结果被人“精准狙击”。有时候那些内幕交易者后来又把钱吐了回来，因为 SEC（美国证监会）找上了他们。他的态度大概是：“是啊，但我们是个做市商，这就是我们的活儿。”

turns.en: We have to do it.
turns.zh: “我们必须做。”

turns.en: We can't just be like, oh, that's a big trade.
turns.zh: “我们不能一看到一笔大单就说‘哦，那是一笔大交易’（就不做了）。”

turns.en: We can't do it. They're not going to not do it, but they surely have some higher order thought about it.
turns.zh: “我们不能不做。”他们不可能不做，但他们肯定对此有某种更高一层的考量。

turns.en: Right. But then the other thing is, and I've written about this, like the simple story here is that people kept coming to Susquehanna to buy puts and Susquehanna kept selling them the puts and then it was short a lot of puts and then like bad stuff happened and I lost a lot of money. But that's not like true. Like that's one part of the story. But the other part of the story is like they're an options market maker. Options market makers like just naturally immediately hedge. Not always. It's not like, but like for the most part, if you sell put options, you then go and short some stock to hedge your risk on the put options. But that's not the only possible hedge. You could lay off the put options, right? That you could sell a hundred put options to a customer and then buy back a hundred put options from other customers or from another market maker or something like that.
turns.zh: 对。但另一件事是——这个我也写过——这里简单的说法是：不断有人来找 Susquehanna 买看跌期权，Susquehanna 不断卖给他们，于是它做空了一大堆看跌期权，然后坏事发生了，它亏了一大笔。但这并不属实，这只是故事的一部分。另一部分是：他们是期权做市商，而期权做市商天然会立即对冲。不是每次都这样，但大体上，你卖出看跌期权后，就会去做空一些股票，来对冲你在看跌期权上的风险。但那不是唯一可能的对冲方式。你也可以把这些看跌期权“甩出去”（lay off）：你可以卖给某个客户 100 份看跌期权，然后再从其他客户、或另一家做市商那里买回 100 份看跌期权，诸如此类。

turns.en: Right.
turns.zh: 对。

turns.en: And so if you're a Cisco head and you're bringing this lawsuit, You're counting each put option that you sold to a customer and saying, this customer was maybe insider trading, so they should give us the money back. But you're only counting those. You're not counting the put options you bought.
turns.zh: 所以如果你是 Susquehanna 的负责人、要提起这场诉讼，你在清点你卖给客户的每一份看跌期权，说“这个客户也许在内幕交易，所以他们该把钱还给我们”。但你只算了这些，没算你买回来的那些看跌期权。

turns.en: Right, right.
turns.zh: 对，对。

turns.en: Because those aren't insider trading. And so, okay, it's certain that they're partially hedged, right? Sure. And the judge quotes them admitting in the court papers, like, yeah, we don't deny hedging, but that goes to damages. We'll discuss that later, right?
turns.zh: 因为那些不算内幕交易。好，所以可以确定他们做了部分对冲。当然。法官还引用了他们在法庭文件中承认的话：“是的，我们不否认做了对冲，但那涉及的是损害赔偿金额，我们以后再谈。”对吧？

turns.en: Yeah, yeah.
turns.zh: 嗯，嗯。

turns.en: But the customers made on the order of $ 70 million. This is what they allege. So Susquehanna lost $ 70 million just on those trades, right? Just on the puts that they sold to the customers. How much did they make on their hedges? It would be shocking if it was less than $ 35 million, right? But it would not be shocking if it was more than $ 70 million, right? There's no allegation that they were like, net short these puts, right? They're buying some puts from some people, selling some puts to some other people. Maybe, maybe they made money that day. I don't know. But they still can sue for the money they lost.
turns.zh: 但这些客户赚了大约 7000 万美元——这是他们的指控。所以说，Susquehanna 光在这些交易上、光在卖给客户的这些看跌期权上，就亏了 7000 万美元。那他们在对冲上赚了多少？如果少于 3500 万美元，那才叫惊人；但如果超过 7000 万美元，也不奇怪，对吧？并没有任何指控说他们是净做空（net short）这些看跌期权的。他们从一些人手里买看跌期权，又卖给另一些人看跌期权。也许，也许他们那天其实是赚钱的，我不知道。但他们仍然可以就自己亏掉的钱提起诉讼。

turns.en: Sure, sure, sure. But it's slightly obscuring the fact that they were also having a hand Right.
turns.zh: 当然，当然，当然。但这多少掩盖了一个事实：他们自己也在其中插了一手。对吧。

turns.en: Like what I wrote is that like, okay, so like Citadel Securities, another big options market maker, joined Susquehanna. They're like, we also sold options.
turns.zh: 我写的是这样：好，Citadel Securities（另一家大型期权做市商）也加入了 Susquehanna 一方。他们说：“我们也卖了期权。”

turns.en: Yeah, yeah, yeah.
turns.zh: 嗯，嗯，嗯。

turns.en: And we also got taken by this, right?
turns.zh: “我们也被这事坑了。”对吧？

turns.en: Pity them.
turns.zh: 真替他们惋惜。

turns.en: So both Citadel Securities and Susquehanna were selling options that day, right? Because they're market makers, right? Also, they were both presumably hedging. I don't know how they hatched. Classically, you delta hedge, you sell some stock, right? So maybe they just sold stock. But it's very possible that if you sell a lot of options, you'll be like, I'm going to buy back some options, right? Maybe they just have customer flow both ways. They have customers buying, they have customers selling, so they buy back from the customers who are selling. Maybe not, though. Maybe one or both of these market makers was like, we have sold a lot of put options. We don't like our risk position. Let's buy back some put options. put a bid in the market. It's not impossible that like Citadel Securities bought some put options from SIG or that SIG.
turns.zh: 所以那天 Citadel Securities 和 Susquehanna 都在卖期权，因为他们是做市商。而且他们想必都在对冲。我不知道他们具体怎么对冲的。经典做法是 delta 对冲，卖出一些股票。所以也许他们就是卖了股票。但如果你卖出很多期权，很可能你会想“我要买回一些期权”。也许他们的客户流本来就是双向的：有客户买，也有客户卖，于是他们从那些在卖的客户手里买回来。但也可能不是。也许这两家做市商中的一家或两家想的是：“我们卖了太多看跌期权，不喜欢自己现在的风险敞口，得买回一些看跌期权，在市场上挂个买价（bid）。”所以，Citadel Securities 从 SIG 手里买了一些看跌期权，或者 SIG——这并非不可能。

turns.en: Bought some put options from Citadel.
turns.zh: 从 Citadel 手里买了一些看跌期权。

turns.en: Securities, right? And then like you have a mess, right? And it's like they should be suing each other. So I don't have any evidence.
turns.zh: ——Securities 手里买，对吧？那样一来就是一团乱麻了，搞得像是他们应该互相起诉对方。所以我并没有任何证据。

turns.en: Some of the John Does are named.
turns.zh: 有些“无名氏”是有名字的。

turns.en: I don't have any evidence of that happened, but like it's, you know, totally possible part of the story, right? It's not like everyone who was buying put options that day was an insider trader, right? Like some of them were, you know, just people in the market. Like possibly... Pacing the frontier.
turns.zh: 我并没有证据说这事真发生了，但它完全可能是故事的一部分。那天买看跌期权的人，不可能个个都是内幕交易者。其中一些人，你知道，就是市场里的普通人。也许……“Pacing the Frontier”（在前沿踱步）。

turns.en: Pacing the frontier. What a terrible... You should talk about that.
turns.zh: “Pacing the Frontier”。这标题真是……你该聊聊这个。

turns.en: No, it's great.
turns.zh: 不，我觉得挺好。

turns.en: Pacing is one of those verbs where it could mean either one, right? Like tabling?
turns.zh: “Pacing”（踱步／控制节奏）是那种可以有两种相反含义的动词，对吧？就像“tabling”（搁置／提上议程）一样？

turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 对。

turns.en: They mean it to say slowing down.
turns.zh: 他们用它是要表达“放慢速度”。

turns.en: Sure.
turns.zh: 当然。

turns.en: But pacing can also mean keeping up with, like in a running.
turns.zh: 但“pacing”也可以指“跟上节奏”，就像跑步里的配速员。

turns.en: To me, pacing as a verb mainly means like walking back and forth because you're nervous.
turns.zh: 对我来说，“pacing”作动词，主要意思是因为紧张而走来走去。

turns.en: Oh, huh.
turns.zh: 哦，嗯。

turns.en: Like you're pacing.
turns.zh: 就是你在来回踱步。

turns.en: Pacing the frontier, like, oh, oh no.
turns.zh: “在前沿来回踱步”，哦，哦不。

turns.en: Oh, the air is going to kill us.
turns.zh: “哦，AI 要杀掉我们所有人了。”

turns.en: It's going to kill us all. It's going to turn us into paperclips. Right.
turns.zh: “它会把我们全杀光，把我们变成回形针。”对。

turns.en: No, anyway, sorry. Dario Amadei.
turns.zh: 不，总之，抱歉。Dario Amodei——

turns.en: Furiously walking back and forth on the frontier. Wearing a cowboy hat.
turns.zh: “在前沿疯狂地来回踱步，头戴一顶牛仔帽。”

turns.en: The CEO of Anthropic. published an essay over the weekend called Pacing the Frontier, basically being like, we should slow down, take a deep breath, and take our time a little bit on the continuing development of frontier AI models because otherwise they might kill us all. I don't think he said otherwise they might kill us all, but that was kind of implied.
turns.zh: Anthropic 的 CEO 周末发表了一篇文章，题为《Pacing the Frontier》，大意是说：我们应该放慢脚步，深吸一口气，在继续开发前沿 AI 模型这件事上从容一点，否则它们可能会把我们全杀光。我不认为他真说了“否则它们可能会把我们全杀光”，但那意思多少是隐含在里面的。

turns.en: Well, this is, to be fair, sort of like the founding, theoretically, was supposed to be the founding ethos of, at the time, OpenAI, which Dario Amadei was a part of. I'm in the middle of reading Kevin Roos' AGI Chronicles, and... First of all, all of them all used to work together at the same place, whether it was Google or OpenAI. But they all, Dario Amadei especially, their main thing was like, we're so concerned with how AI is going to potentially ruin everything. So we need to be the ones to do it so that Google doesn't do it.
turns.zh: 公平地说，这本该是当年 OpenAI 理论上的立身之本，而 Dario Amodei 曾是其中一员。我正在读 Kevin Roose 的《AGI Chronicles》（AGI 编年史）……首先，这些人以前都在同一个地方共事过，不管是谷歌还是 OpenAI。但他们所有人——尤其是 Dario Amodei——的核心主张是：“我们太担心 AI 可能会毁掉一切了，所以必须由我们来做这件事，好让谷歌做不成。”

turns.en: Every AI developer is someone who's worried about AI killing us all.
turns.zh: 每个 AI 开发者，都是那种担心 AI 会把我们全杀光的人。

turns.en: That's like the main identity.
turns.zh: 那基本就是他们的核心身份认同。

turns.en: You can't get into AI without starting from the thought.
turns.zh: 你没法不从这个念头出发就进入 AI 行业——

turns.en: What if AI kills us all? Exactly. Right. That is the number one starting point.
turns.zh: “万一 AI 把我们全杀光了呢？”正是。对。这就是头号出发点。

turns.en: There's so much about this essay. So many people are being like, this is all cynical marketing, and they don't believe this.
turns.zh: 关于这篇文章有太多可说的了。很多人都在讲：这全是玩世不恭的营销，他们自己并不信。

turns.en: What if it's genuine marketing?
turns.zh: 那如果这是“真诚的营销”呢？

turns.en: People have different views on this, but I think there's clearly a marketing benefit to conveying how powerful your AI is by saying, oh, what if it goes a little? I think, is there cynicism in the AI industry? Is Sam Altman being somewhat cynical? Maybe.
turns.zh: 对此人们看法不一，但我认为，通过“哦，万一它有点失控了呢？”这种说法来传达你的 AI 有多强大，显然有营销上的好处。我是说，AI 行业里有没有玩世不恭的成分？Sam Altman 是不是有点玩世不恭？也许吧。

turns.en: Sam is a different person.
turns.zh: Sam 那是另一个人的问题（另当别论）。

turns.en: Do I think that most people at The big AI labs are genuinely worried about AI killing us all? Yes. I don't think it's all marketing. Right.
turns.zh: 我是否认为大型 AI 实验室里的大多数人是真心担心 AI 会把我们全杀光？是的。我不认为这全是营销。对。

turns.en: No, that's like, you definitely get that sense reading Kevin's book that like, that's the starting point for everyone is like, oh my God, this is so powerful. It's going to obliterate us. How do we control it? Also, I need to be first. Right. It's very paradoxical.
turns.zh: 不，读 Kevin 那本书你绝对会有这种感觉：对每个人来说，出发点都是“我的天，这东西太强大了，它会把我们抹掉。我们该怎么控制它？”同时——“而且我得做第一个。”对。这非常矛盾。

turns.en: I joke about this because like, I think a lot about how much AI researchers get paid. Oh God.
turns.zh: 我拿这个开玩笑，是因为我会想很多关于 AI 研究员薪水的问题。天哪。

turns.en: And how- More than- everything.
turns.zh: 还有他们——比谁都多——什么都比。

turns.en: Right. And like how in the financial industry, there's like a traditional, like people have their number, right? And if you get paid $ 30 million, you can stop working. And not everyone, right? But like you need some method of motivating people to continue working.
turns.zh: 对。以及在金融行业，有个传统说法：每个人都有自己的“那个数”（number）。如果你拿到 3000 万美元，你就可以不干了。当然不是每个人都这样，但你需要某种办法来激励人们继续工作。

turns.en: But they don't care about money. Well, they do and they don't.
turns.zh: 但他们不在乎钱。——嗯，他们既在乎又不在乎。

turns.en: The fact that they get paid $ 30 million just proves that they do.
turns.zh: 他们能拿到 3000 万美元这件事，本身就证明了他们在乎。

turns.en: Isn't it like 75 sometimes?
turns.zh: 有时候不是有 7500 万吗？

turns.en: Whatever, yeah. I mean, it's huge numbers. But like the point is that In the financial industry, people think very hard about how to calibrate salaries so that you keep working even.
turns.zh: 随便啦，对。我是说，都是巨额数字。但关键在于：在金融行业，人们会非常认真地琢磨怎么校准薪酬，好让你即便——

turns.en: Though you're making $ 30 million a year.
turns.zh: ——即便你一年赚 3000 万美元，也继续干下去。

turns.en: And I don't understand how it works in AI. And I have joked that one way it works is that because the AI researchers believe that their product will kill everyone on Earth, that is somehow motivating. I see. So it's not the money.
turns.zh: 而我不明白 AI 行业是怎么运作的。我开玩笑说，其中一种运作方式是：正因为 AI 研究员相信自己的产品会杀光地球上的每个人，这在某种程度上反而成了激励。——我明白了。所以驱动他们的不是钱。

turns.en: It's the singularity.
turns.zh: 是“奇点”（singularity）。

turns.en: Yeah. And I've joked that when I worked at Goldman, if you had told everyone that our work was going to kill everyone on Earth, That would probably not make us more of a way to do it. But then I thought about it for a minute. I was like, well, maybe, maybe, maybe.
turns.zh: 对。我还开玩笑说，当年我在高盛（Goldman）时，如果有人告诉大家“我们的工作会杀光地球上的每个人”，那大概不会让我们更想干这行。但后来我想了想，又觉得：嗯，也许，也许，也许还真会。

turns.en: It's going to be the derivative.
turns.zh: “要杀人的是那些衍生品（derivative）。”

turns.en: But it's just like a weird, right. A weird culture of everyone being like, oh man, I'm so excited to go to work at the Killing Everyone on Earth factory today. But yeah.
turns.zh: 但这就是很怪，对吧。一种很怪的文化：人人都在说“哦老兄，我今天超兴奋，要去‘杀光地球上每个人工厂’上班了”。不过是啊。

turns.en: Okay. So Dario wrote this memo where he's like, we got to hold hands and not kill us all.
turns.zh: 好。所以 Dario 写了这份备忘录，意思是：“我们得手拉手，别把我们全杀光。”

turns.en: Right. So. if you want to be cynical, there's like a very simple cynical story, which is that like, like one model for what's going on in AI is that the model capabilities are kind of ahead of deployment in a lot of areas, right? Like there's just like so much stuff where companies could add economic value by using existing AI models that they just haven't gotten around to yet. Cause like it's too new and they're not trained on it and they need more forward deployed engineers to like, you know, so you have like, Anthropic and OpenAI doing all these partnerships with private equity firms to basically roll out AI to companies, right? So if you just turned off model development for the next year, Anthropic and OpenAI could do a lot of business. They could sell a lot of products, right? And they'd make a lot of money because their unit economics are pretty good.
turns.zh: 对。所以如果你想玩世不恭一点，有一个非常简单的犬儒式解释：对 AI 现状的一种理解是，在很多领域，模型的能力其实领先于落地部署。也就是说，有大量场景，公司本可以通过使用现有的 AI 模型创造经济价值，只是它们还没顾得上——因为太新了，员工没受过相关培训，还需要更多“前置部署工程师”（forward deployed engineers）。所以你会看到 Anthropic 和 OpenAI 跟私募股权公司搞了这么多合作，基本上是把 AI 推广到各家企业。那么，如果在接下来一年里干脆关掉模型开发，Anthropic 和 OpenAI 也能做很多生意、卖很多产品，赚很多钱，因为它们的单位经济模型（unit economics）相当不错。

turns.en: That's going to work at the making... Money factory. That's not going to work at the killing everyone factory.
turns.zh: 这在“赚钱工厂”那边行得通，在“杀光所有人工厂”那边就行不通了。

turns.en: Like AI right now is in kind of a great place, which is that it's commercially useful.
turns.zh: 现在的 AI 处在一个挺美妙的位置：它在商业上是有用的。

turns.en: There's all these applications.
turns.zh: 有这么多应用场景。

turns.en: It has barely scratched the surface of its commercial use. I mean, people will disagree with that, but I think a lot of people think that. And it's probably not going to kill us all right this second. And so what a great place to be. But because there is a competitive pressure to build the best model every frontier lab, instead of only just going around sending out forward deployed engineers to like sell more compute to accounting firms is spending bajillions of dollars training their next model. And will the next model kill us all?
turns.zh: 它在商业应用上才刚刚触及皮毛。我是说，会有人不同意，但我觉得很多人是这么想的。而且它眼下大概还不会立刻把我们全杀光。所以这是个多好的位置啊。可是，由于存在“必须做出最好模型”的竞争压力，每一家前沿实验室——而不是只派前置部署工程师到处跑、给会计师事务所多卖点算力——都在砸下天文数字的钱去训练它们的下一个模型。那么，下一个模型会把我们全杀光吗？

turns.en: Right. They're on the frontier specifically seeking AGI.
turns.zh: 对。他们在前沿，专门在追求 AGI（通用人工智能）。

turns.en: Sure.
turns.zh: 当然。

turns.en: Trying to get to whatever point.
turns.zh: 试图抵达某个临界点。

turns.en: But like, but like, so right.
turns.zh: 但是，但是，所以对。

turns.en: So one, you can have the factory doing the making money over here, but everyone always needs to have the engineers at the frontier. Like the competition is like still being the best.
turns.zh: 所以，第一，你可以让“赚钱工厂”在这边运转，但每个人都始终需要把工程师放在前沿。因为竞争的核心还是“要做最好的那个”。

turns.en: Yeah. But like, but like one aspect of that is like that competition might lead to robots that kill us all. regardless of that, that competition is very expensive. It requires a lot.
turns.zh: 对。但这一点的一个方面是：这种竞争可能会带来把我们全杀光的机器人。且不论这个，这种竞争本身就极其昂贵，需要大量——

turns.en: Of data centers, right?
turns.zh: ——数据中心，对吧？

turns.en: It requires a lot of training.
turns.zh: 需要大量训练。

turns.en: So many chips.
turns.zh: 需要海量芯片。

turns.en: And if you just turned off that competition, first of all, we'd have one more year before robots kill us all. But second of all, they'd be much more profitable, right? And so the simple cynical story is that the frontier AI labs would have a better business if they didn't have to race to train their models, right? Right.
turns.zh: 如果你干脆关掉这种竞争，第一，我们能多出一年的时间，才轮到机器人来杀光我们；第二，它们的盈利能力会强得多。所以那个简单的犬儒式解释就是：前沿 AI 实验室如果不必争分夺秒地训练模型，生意会更好，对吧？对。

turns.en: So there's a business case you're saying for what Amadeus Yeah.
turns.zh: 所以你是说，Amodei 的主张背后是有商业逻辑的。——对。

turns.en: And by the way, the biggest critic of this is Donald Trump, who called Jensen Huang to be like, it's a hoax. Donald Trump saying something is a hoax is the most terrifying thing I've heard about AI existential risk. But no, another critic of it is Jensen Huang, who does not run a Frontier ALAP. Right.
turns.zh: 顺便说一句，对此最大的批评者是 Donald Trump，他打电话给黄仁勋（Jensen Huang）说“这是个骗局”。Donald Trump 说某件事是骗局，这是我听过的关于 AI 生存风险最恐怖的事了。不过，另一个批评者是黄仁勋本人，而他并不经营一家前沿 AI 实验室。对。

turns.en: He's the chip man.
turns.zh: 他是那个“芯片大佬”。

turns.en: He sells chips. And his business is much better if they're constantly training the next model and buying new chips. So he is a critic of this for straightforward. I mean, I think that everyone has genuine beliefs. Sure. But also, like, his straightforward business interests are in racing to train models as much as possible. And Dario's and Sam Albin's are maybe not doing that. The other thing I wrote about is like, okay, so like arguably OpenAI and Anthropic have some business interest in not training models that fast so that they can, you know, capture some revenue from their existing models. And as several people, including David Sack said, you can just not, you just do that. You don't have to train the next model that will kill us all. You can just not do that. But there is competitive pressure to train the next model that will kill us all because one, Some customers want the most advanced model, and it really helps to be on the top of the leaderboard of who's got the best model. And then two, you're competing for researchers too, and the researchers want to be at the best lab, not the worst lab.
turns.zh: 他卖芯片。如果这些公司不停地训练下一个模型、不停地买新芯片，他的生意就好得多。所以他批评这事，是出于非常直白的——我是说，我觉得每个人都有真诚的信念，当然——但同样地，他直白的商业利益就在于“尽可能争分夺秒地训练模型”。而 Dario 和 Sam Altman 的利益也许并不在此。我写的另一件事是：好，可以说 OpenAI 和 Anthropic 有某种商业动机不那么快地训练模型，好从现有模型里多榨取一些收入。而且正如包括 David Sacks 在内的好几个人说的：你完全可以不干啊，就这么着呗。你并非非得去训练那个会杀光我们的下一个模型，你可以选择不做。但确实存在竞争压力，逼着你去训练那个会杀光我们的下一个模型，因为：第一，有些客户就是想要最先进的模型，而稳居“谁家模型最强”排行榜榜首真的很有帮助；第二，你还要争夺研究员，而研究员想去最好的实验室，不想去最差的。

turns.en: It feels like a crucible of capitalism.
turns.zh: 这感觉像是资本主义的一个熔炉（试炼场）。

turns.en: Right. The interesting thing is that because there are competitive pressures, no one entirely feels like they can unilaterally disarm. But there's some chance that if you got the four leading AI labs in a room, they could agree to disarm. Right. And there's other non frontier competitors who could catch up to them, but maybe it'd be okay. But if you got like the four competitors in a room and they agreed to like slow the rollout of their products. that looks like a very classic antitrust conspiracy and so it's not clear they can do.
turns.zh: 对。有意思的是，正因为存在竞争压力，没有谁真的觉得自己能单方面“裁军”。但如果把四家顶尖 AI 实验室关进一个房间，它们倒是有可能达成“裁军”协议。当然，还有其他非前沿的竞争者可能追上来，但也许没关系。可问题是，如果把这四家竞争者凑到一个房间里、让它们商定放慢产品的推出，那看起来就是非常经典的反垄断合谋（antitrust conspiracy），所以它们能不能这么干并不清楚。

turns.en: That and so conspiracy to save humanity well this is the thing.
turns.zh: 那……于是就成了“为拯救人类而合谋”。嗯，这就说到点子上了。

turns.en: Like so i read about this like there's this amazing lawsuit it's like against blackrock because.
turns.zh: 我读到过这个——有一场特别精彩的诉讼，是告贝莱德（BlackRock）的，因为——

turns.en: It's like yeah it's incomprehensible but.
turns.zh: 是啊，简直让人无法理解，但——

turns.en: Like basically there's this idea that like ESG investors led by BlackRock, tell coal companies to stop producing coal. And why do they tell coal companies to stop producing coal? Well, they will tell you because coal creates pollution and climate change and is bad for us. And so as responsible stewards of capital and of the environment, they would like to produce less coal. But the plaintiffs in this lawsuit, which is several state attorney generals, They say maybe, but the effect of telling coal companies to produce less coal is that coal prices go up. And the coal companies have- Colluded. Yeah. Essentially, you have a cartel to sell less coal at higher prices. It's like OPEC for coal. And the takeaway from this lawsuit is that even if you have a good pro-humanity reason for conspiring to restrict the supply of your product, it's still potentially an antitrust conspiracy.
turns.zh: 基本的说法是：以贝莱德为首的 ESG 投资者，让煤炭公司停止产煤。他们为什么要煤炭公司少产煤呢？他们会告诉你：因为煤会造成污染和气候变化，对我们有害；所以作为资本和环境的负责任管理者，他们希望少产煤。但这起诉讼的原告——是几位州总检察长——他们说：也许是吧，但“让煤炭公司少产煤”的效果，是煤价上涨。而这些煤炭公司已经——“串通”了。对。本质上，你有一个卡特尔（cartel），以更少的产量、更高的价格卖煤，就像煤炭版的 OPEC。而这起诉讼给人的启示是：即便你合谋限制自家产品供应是出于一个利人类的正当理由，它仍然可能构成反垄断合谋。

turns.en: And I quote, trying to save the world is no excuse for an antitrust conspiracy.
turns.zh: 我引用一下你的话：“试图拯救世界，不能作为反垄断合谋的借口。”

turns.en: Right. And, like, by the way, that has to be wrong. Like, obviously, trying to save the world is a very good excuse for an antitrust conspiracy.
turns.zh: 对。顺便说一句，这话肯定是错的。显然，“试图拯救世界”是反垄断合谋的一个非常好的借口。

turns.en: Yeah, the main excuse.
turns.zh: 对，是头号借口。

turns.en: Yeah. Maybe not under, like, traditional antitrust law. But, like, if you're like, the robots were an hour away from killing everyone on Earth, so I'd... Turn them off. Me and the CEO of my competitor held hands and turned them off. Like, great, do that. Yeah. And then you go to jail for antitrust conspiracy.
turns.zh: 对。也许在传统反垄断法下不算。但如果情况是：“机器人再过一小时就要杀光地球上的每个人了，所以我……把它们关了。我和竞争对手的 CEO 手拉手把它们关了。”那——太好了，就该这么干。是啊。然后你就因为反垄断合谋去坐牢。

turns.en: Worth it.
turns.zh: 值了。

turns.en: But, right, like... So Darius SA does have a footnote being like, with appropriate changes to antitrust law, right? They need permission to get together in a room to agree to.
turns.zh: 但是，对……所以 Dario 的文章里确实有一个脚注，说“在对反垄断法做适当修改的前提下”。他们需要获准聚到一个房间里，去商定——

turns.en: Turn off the killer alerts. Right, which is why you wrote that they can't just do it themselves. They sort of need the government to nod at them and say.
turns.zh: ——关掉那些“杀手机器人”。对，这正是你写到的：他们没法自己单干，多少需要政府对他们点点头，说……

turns.en: Yeah, but it's like this weird situation where the people building AI are like, this is going to kill us all.
turns.zh: 对，但这是个很怪的局面：造 AI 的人在说“这会杀光我们所有人”——

turns.en: And Donald Trump is like, no, it's a hoax.
turns.zh: ——而 Donald Trump 说：“不，这是个骗局。”

turns.en: So I don't think they're going to get regulated.
turns.zh: 所以我不觉得他们会受到监管。

turns.en: A couple of things that are really interesting about the Kevin Ruse book, which I'm only halfway through, but one of the really amazing.
turns.zh: 关于 Kevin Roose 那本书，有几件事特别有意思——我才读了一半——但其中一个真正令人惊叹的……

turns.en: Is it out by the way?
turns.zh: 顺便问一句，它出版了吗？

turns.en: It is not out. The publication date is October 6th. I got an advanced copy because, you know, I edit a newsletter. But one of the more interesting... I mean, it is a sort of narrative history of how we got here and the race to AGI. And something that is really kind of funny to me is Amadei's Pacing the Frontier memo. Like, the entire book is like, oh, and then there was the big this memo, and then the big that memo, and the say AGI memo, and the all of these instances are marked by documents written by humans, which is so interesting to me because all that we talk about now with AI is like, oh, was it written with AI? The foundational inflection points and dramatic tensions in the book, every moment there is an associated memo.
turns.zh: 还没出。出版日期是 10 月 6 日。我拿到了提前样书，因为你知道，我是编辑通讯的。但更有意思的一点是……这本书算是讲述“我们如何走到今天”以及这场 AGI 竞赛的一部叙事史。而让我觉得特别好玩的是 Amodei 那份《Pacing the Frontier》备忘录。整本书都是这种调调：“哦，然后有了那份重要的备忘录，接着又有那份重要的备忘录，还有那份 AGI 备忘录……”所有这些关键节点，都是由人类写下的文件来标记的——这对我太有意思了，因为我们现在谈 AI 时，张口就是“哦，这是不是 AI 写的？”书里那些奠基性的拐点和戏剧性张力，每一个时刻都对应着一份备忘录。

turns.en: I was thinking about that. I find myself really allergic to writing that sounds like stereotypical AI writing. And so as I was reading Daria's memo, I was like, did Clara write this?
turns.zh: 我也在想这个。我发现自己对那种听起来像典型 AI 写作的文字真的很“过敏”。所以我在读 Dario 那份备忘录时，心里想：这是 Claude 写的吗？

turns.en: And I'm like, no, it doesn't sound like AI at all.
turns.zh: 而我想的是：不，它一点都不像 AI 写的。

turns.en: All of these people are good writers.
turns.zh: 这些人都是好写手。

turns.en: Yes, no, there is zero. I mean, they're all philosophers, right? And that's like the most of what they're doing is they're getting together. They all live in this one house on Delano Street or whatever. And they're all like talking and staying up through the night. And like, they all write these original foundational pieces of text. And I just think it's just such an interesting idea that like some of the most important documents of like the race to building this thing that is intelligent are these like human handwritten hand sewn hand forged you know flags planted in the ground about you know this must be done or in order to do this this is where we are this is a watershed moment yeah.
turns.zh: 是的，不，一点 AI 味都没有。我是说，他们都是哲学家，对吧？他们做的大部分事情，就是聚在一起。他们都住在某条“德拉诺街”之类的一栋房子里，一起聊天、通宵达旦。然后他们每个人都写下这些原创的、奠基性的文本。我就是觉得这个想法特别有意思：在“造出这个有智能的东西”这场竞赛中，一些最重要的文件，竟然是这些人类亲手写、亲手缝、亲手锻造的旗帜——插在地上宣告“此事必须做”，或者“为了做成这件事，我们正处在此地，这是一个分水岭时刻”。是啊。

turns.en: But that's just like just we're just in like a like a phase transition right like most of the code most of the algorithms behind modern ai are were invented by humans because who else would have done it, right? But like now we're at a point of recursive self-improvement where like now like the AI is programming the AI. All these people grew up in a, they didn't grow up in a world where AI would write papers for them. And like they've thought a lot about this. And the idea of going to Claude and being like, write a memo about restricting Claude is stupid. But like the next generation will just do that. They'll be like, hey Claude, what should I do?
turns.zh: 但我们只是正处在一场“相变”（phase transition）之中：现代 AI 背后的大多数代码、大多数算法都是人类发明的，因为还能有谁来做呢，对吧？但现在我们已经走到了“递归式自我改进”（recursive self-improvement）这一步，是 AI 在给 AI 编程。这些人成长于——或者说，他们并没有成长在一个 AI 会替他们写文章的世界里，而他们对这一点思考了很多。跑去让 Claude“写一份关于限制 Claude 的备忘录”，这想法很蠢。但下一代人就会这么干。他们会说：“嘿 Claude，我该怎么办？”

turns.en: I think Claude will be great at that.
turns.zh: 我觉得 Claude 会很擅长这个。

turns.en: He'll be like, no, like great for like, Claude will do a perfectly adequate job.
turns.zh: 他会——不，我是说，“擅长”……Claude 会干得完全称职、够用。

turns.en: We won't need to write the memos because Claude will already be our overlord. I know.
turns.zh: 我们压根不用写备忘录了，因为到时候 Claude 已经是我们的霸主了。我知道。

turns.en: Like Claude will do a perfectly adequate job of laying out the reasons for restricting the pace of AI improvement, but not stylishly. No, no.
turns.zh: 我是说，Claude 会完全称职地把“为什么要限制 AI 进步速度”的理由列出来，但不会写得有风格。不不不。

turns.en: I mean, unless you trained it on, you know, some of the most stylish writing out there, like money stuff columns.
turns.zh: 我是说，除非你拿世上最有风格的文字去训练它，比如《Money Stuff》专栏。

turns.en: Claude has ingested a lot of money stuff.
turns.zh: Claude 已经吞下了不少《Money Stuff》。

turns.en: Claude has ingested all of it. Let's talk about pensions.
turns.zh: Claude 已经把它全吞了。我们来聊聊养老金吧。

turns.en: Okay.
turns.zh: 好。

turns.en: I was told that this was a thing that used to exist. You used to have a job in one place for 40 years. And then you would retire. And in exchange, you got a pension at the end.
turns.zh: 有人告诉我，养老金是曾经存在过的东西。你过去会在一个地方干 40 年，然后退休，作为交换，你最后能拿到一份养老金。

turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 对。

turns.en: It was very simple. Everyone had them. The world worked.
turns.zh: 非常简单。人人都有。世界照常运转。

turns.en: Right. There were some problems with it. One of them is that if you didn't have a job for 40 years, if you moved jobs, pensions were more complicated. Another problem is actually like there's this like notion of a golden age where everyone had a defined benefit pension, but like, in fact, like the majority of people did not have defined benefit pensions. And then another problem is that occasionally pensions would go bankrupt, right? Because the idea of a pension fund is like, you know, you work at a company, the company agrees to pay you some number of dollars, some formula, something every month after you retire. And how it meets those obligations is like sort of in the first instance up to the company. And so it like sets aside some money and invests it. And if it invests it in dumb stuff and loses all the money, then you don't get your pension, which is bad. And so like ERISA, the retirement security law was passed to kind of clamp down on pension fund bankruptcies. But there was a set stream of liabilities. And so the company had to invest to meet those liabilities. And over time in the U.S., that has been like largely replaced by like the 401k.
turns.zh: 对。但它有一些问题。其一，如果你没有一份干满 40 年的工作，如果你换工作，养老金就变复杂了。另一个问题其实是：人们有种“黄金年代”的观念，以为人人都有固定收益型（defined benefit）养老金，但事实上，大多数人并没有固定收益型养老金。还有一个问题是，养老金偶尔会破产。因为养老金的逻辑是：你在一家公司工作，公司答应在你退休后每月按某个公式、某个数额付你钱。而公司如何履行这些义务，起初基本上由公司自己决定。于是它拨出一笔钱去投资。如果它投了些蠢东西、把钱亏光，你就拿不到养老金了，这就糟了。所以《雇员退休收入保障法》（ERISA）出台，多少是为了遏制养老金破产。但那是一串固定的负债，公司必须投资以覆盖这些负债。而随着时间推移，在美国，这在很大程度上被 401(k) 取代了。

turns.en: Why did that happen? What was wrong with the defined benefit pension besides the fact that it sort of never really existed in this imaginary wonderful way that we thought?
turns.zh: 为什么会这样？除了“它从未真的以我们想象中那种美好方式存在过”之外，固定收益型养老金到底有什么毛病？

turns.en: Well, a couple of reasons. One is that if you're moving jobs, like a 401k is yours.
turns.zh: 嗯，有几个原因。一是如果你换工作，401(k) 是属于你自己的。

turns.en: Yeah, you're like, wait, I need to leave this company to go to different jobs. But like you can't take your pension with you.
turns.zh: 对，你会想：“等等，我要离开这家公司去别处工作，可你没法把养老金一起带走。”

turns.en: Right, because the pension like belongs to the company. So it's complicated to have a pension if you're moving jobs a lot. Whereas a 401k, you can move with you. It's just an account that belongs to you. Another reason is that the pension itself is a risk, right? Because there is a mismatch between the company has promised you a monthly dollar amount of benefits, and those benefits are 20 years in the future. And so it has to invest such that it will be able to meet that dollar amount of benefits.
turns.zh: 对，因为养老金属于公司。所以如果你频繁换工作，持有养老金就很麻烦。而 401(k) 可以跟着你走，它就是一个属于你的账户。另一个原因是，养老金本身就是一种风险：公司承诺了你每月一笔固定数额的福利，而这笔福利是 20 年以后的事，两者之间存在错配。所以公司必须投资，以确保将来能兑现那个数额的福利。

turns.en: Better get it right.
turns.zh: 最好别算错。

turns.en: Yeah. One way to do that is to buy treasury bonds that will pay out exactly the amount of benefits, but that's very expensive, right? Another way to do it is to buy stocks that you hope will grow to meet the amount of benefits. Don't get it wrong. But you have, there's risk there. The thing about a 401k is that it's not, in the general case, a promised stream of benefits. It's just a dollar amount. It's just a big pool. Yeah. So if you put money in a 401k, you have the money in the 401k. If the stocks go down, they go down. But there's no, like, funding gap, right? Right. You're never, like, I mean, there is. Sure. There is, right?
turns.zh: 对。一种办法是买国债，让它正好支付福利的数额，但那非常贵。另一种办法是买股票，指望它涨到足以覆盖福利金额。别算错。但这里是有风险的。401(k) 的特点在于：一般情况下，它不是承诺的一串福利，它只是一个金额、一个资金池。所以如果你往 401(k) 里放钱，钱就在 401(k) 里。股票跌了，就是跌了。但不存在那种“资金缺口”（funding gap），对吧？对。你永远不会——我是说，其实是有的。当然。确实有，对吧？

turns.en: Maybe the number is as big as you want.
turns.zh: 也许那个数字可以大到随你想。

turns.en: It to be. Yeah. You can convert. either like literally by buying annuities or just mathematically by like multiplying by 4% or whatever, you can convert your balance in your 401k into a stream of income in retirement. And if that stream of income is not sufficient to support your lifestyle, then you have a funding gap. But it doesn't like look like that. It's not like on financial statements. It's not like a company being like, oh, we have a billion dollar funding gap. It's just like, oh, the number in your 401k is lower than you'd like. So it creates less concentrated risk, right? There's no, you're never gonna have a pension bankruptcy if you have 401ks. But then the other reason And I know this is true, but it's just like a thing people used to say is that the move from pension funds to 401ks was like good for Wall Street, right? Because the idea is that you take all of these people who are like, you know, working and like hoping, you know, counting on a pension for retirement and you turn them into individual investors. You turn them into people who, instead of just like counting on their employer to fund their retirement, they're now playing the stock market and they become customers of wall street.
turns.zh: 它是要……对。你可以转换：要么实打实地通过买年金（annuities），要么纯粹在数学上乘个 4% 之类，把 401(k) 里的余额转换成退休后的一串收入。如果那串收入不足以支撑你的生活方式，那你就有了资金缺口。但它看起来不像那种缺口——它不会出现在财务报表上，不像一家公司说“哦，我们有 10 亿美元的资金缺口”。它只是“哦，你 401(k) 里的数字比你希望的少”。所以它造成的风险不那么集中：只要有 401(k)，你就永远不会遇到养老金破产。但另一个原因——我知道这是真的，只是过去人们常挂在嘴边——是从养老金转向 401(k) 对华尔街是好事。因为这里的逻辑是：你把所有这些一边工作、一边指望靠养老金退休的人，变成个人投资者；把他们变成不再单纯指望雇主为退休买单、而是自己去炒股市的人，于是他们成了华尔街的客户。

turns.en: Right. And they're like, is some part of this also that like, Oh, now I can do the dials on my own 401k.
turns.zh: 对。而且他们会想：这其中是不是也有一部分是“哦，现在我可以自己拨弄我 401(k) 上的那些旋钮了”。

turns.en: Oh yeah, totally. Right. And so not everyone does the dials on their own 401k. Like the most popular 401k investment is target date funds.
turns.zh: 哦是的，完全没错。所以并不是每个人都会自己拨弄 401(k) 的旋钮。最热门的 401(k) 投资是目标日期基金（target date funds）。

turns.en: Set it and forget it.
turns.zh: “一劳永逸”（Set it and forget it）。

turns.en: Yeah. Target date funds, which are truly set it for their, They're like not even index funds. They're like a slider of index funds where it's like, you know, mostly stock index funds and becomes mostly bond index.
turns.zh: 对。目标日期基金，是真正的“设好就不用管”。它们甚至不只是指数基金，而是一个指数基金的“滑动条”：一开始以股票指数基金为主，随着时间推移变成以债券指数——

turns.en: Funds over time. Right.
turns.zh: ——基金为主。对。

turns.en: So it's not turning the dials on your own 401k, but like you could, you could. There's all sorts of like possibilities for investments in 401ks. And so like the idea back in the day was like, oh, this is like creating a lot of customers for Wall Street.
turns.zh: 所以这不是在自己拨弄 401(k) 的旋钮，但你可以，你完全可以。401(k) 里有各种各样的投资可能。所以当年的说法是：“哦，这等于给华尔街创造了一大批客户。”

turns.en: Got it.
turns.zh: 明白了。

turns.en: But what I've argued is that first of all, pensions, it doesn't really create customers for Wall Street because if a company goes from having a pension to having 401ks, Sure, all those 401k investors are now customers of Wall Street.
turns.zh: 但我的论点是：首先，从养老金转向 401(k) 其实并没有真的给华尔街新增客户，因为如果一家公司从有养老金改成有 401(k)，当然，那些 401(k) 投资者现在成了华尔街的客户——

turns.en: Right, it doesn't change the shape of the customers.
turns.zh: 对，但它没有改变客户的“形态”。

turns.en: So you don't have the big pension customer, you have like a thousand small 401k customers. And in some ways that's better for Wall Street because you can sell the 401k customers all sorts of other services.
turns.zh: 你不再有那个庞大的养老金客户，而是有了一千个小小的 401(k) 客户。在某些方面这对华尔街更好，因为你可以向这些 401(k) 客户兜售各种其他服务。

turns.en: More customers.
turns.zh: 更多客户。

turns.en: Yeah, and maybe they'll be less sophisticated customers. in some ways. But the advantage of the pension is it actually turns out to be a really good customer for Wall Street. Because the pension can, because it has a very long time horizon, can do kind of spicy stuff that a retail stock investor wouldn't do. And so pensions are classically great customers for private equity and private credit and all sorts of other investments. And I think that 30 years ago, you would have said, well, probably these retail investors will pay higher fees to Wall Street than a big, sophisticated pension that can bargain for its fees. But what has happened in the last few decades is that the 401k has become just index funds, targeted, cheap indexed. public equity investment and like in fact it turns out retail investors pay very low fees like over time because there has just been a lot of pricing pressure from like indexing and pension funds like sure like they get a volume discount and their indexing is very cheap but like they can do you know put money into a 2 in 20 private equity fund and so the thing that I've been writing about recently is that I feel like there is a financial industry push to like revive the.
turns.zh: 对，而且在某些方面他们可能是没那么老练的客户。但养老金的优势在于，它其实反而是华尔街一个非常好的客户：因为养老金有非常长的时间跨度，可以做那种散户股票投资者不会做的“重口味”投资。所以养老金历来是私募股权（PE）、私募信贷（private credit）等各种投资的绝佳客户。我想 30 年前你会说：这些散户大概会比一个能就费率讨价还价的、老练的大型养老金，向华尔街付更高的费用。但过去几十年发生的是，401(k) 已经变成了纯粹的指数基金——目标日期式的、廉价的指数化公开股票投资；事实上，随着时间推移，散户付的费用非常低，因为指数化带来了巨大的定价压力。而养老金嘛，是的，它们能拿到批量折扣，指数化也很便宜，但它们可以把钱投进“2 加 20”（2 and 20）收费的私募股权基金。所以我最近一直在写的是：我感觉金融行业有一股推动力，想要复兴——

turns.en: Pension fund reinvent the pension fund yeah.
turns.zh: ——养老金。重塑养老金。对。

turns.en: Because like what you see is like this huge push to put private credit and private equity into retirement funds and yep how do you do that well you can just.
turns.zh: 因为你看到的是，有一股巨大的推动力，要把私募信贷和私募股权塞进退休基金里。对。那怎么做呢？你可以直接——

turns.en: You get trump to say it's allowed so.
turns.zh: 你让 Trump 说这是允许的，所以——

turns.en: That happened right legally it's fine you can put whatever you want you put crypto sports betting everything um seriously But there's a question of what vehicle you use. And so you just be like, well, we'll sell private equity to retail investors. How did that go? Well, so I've been writing about this for a while. And you hear people at private asset managers say, look, retirement savers can take some risk. They can take some illiquidity risk because they have a long time horizon. They don't need their money for 30 years, so they should be able to take some illiquidity risk. They should be buying illiquid stuff. They should be buying private equity, private credit that pays some premium in exchange for not being able to sell it that day because they don't need to sell it that day. They're retirement savers. And like that has a certain theoretical appeal. Sure. It's true. And that's why pension funds can do it, right? Pension funds also have 30-year time horizons.
turns.zh: 这事确实发生了。对，法律上没问题，你想放什么都行——加密货币、体育博彩、什么都行，说真的。但问题在于你用什么载体（vehicle）。你可以说：“那我们就把私募股权卖给散户好了。”结果怎么样呢？这事我写了一阵子了。你会听到私募资产管理公司的人说：“瞧，退休储蓄者是能承受一些风险的。他们可以承担一些流动性风险（illiquidity risk），因为他们时间跨度长，30 年都用不上这笔钱，所以应该能承担一些流动性风险，应该去买非流动性的东西——应该去买私募股权、私募信贷，用‘当天卖不掉’换取一些溢价，反正他们也不需要当天卖掉，他们是退休储蓄者嘛。”这在理论上有一定吸引力。当然。这是真的，这也正是养老金能这么做的原因：养老金也有 30 年的时间跨度。

turns.en: But don't people like to, you know, maybe borrow a little bit from their 401k sometimes?
turns.zh: 但人们难道不喜欢……偶尔从自己的 401(k) 里借一点钱出来吗？

turns.en: Yeah, like it turns out that people do want liquidity in their retirement savings, even though like, you know, at some like first principles level they shouldn't because like, yeah, like emergencies happen Or just like the experience of being able to manage your own money means that you might change your mind.
turns.zh: 对，事实证明，人们确实希望自己的退休储蓄有流动性，尽管从某种第一性原理的层面看他们不该这么想——因为，是啊，会有突发状况；或者说，仅仅是“能自己打理自己的钱”这种体验，就意味着你可能会改变主意。

turns.en: You might be like, oh, I want to move to something else.
turns.zh: 你可能会想：“哦，我想换到别的东西上去。”

turns.en: And when you go to a like institutional asset manager and you say, we'll pay you a premium for locking up your money. They're like, oh yes, we understand that. With retail investors, it's somewhat harder to convey that idea. And we've seen that this year with like the private credit PDC stuff where all these private business development companies raise money from retail investors. And they're like, we'll earn a liquidity premium by investing your money in private credit And then there was some bad news about software companies, and all these investors were like, we'd like our money back. And the BDCs were like, no, no, you're not supposed to.
turns.zh: 而当你去找一个机构资产管理人说“你锁定资金，我们付你溢价”，他们会说“哦是的，我们懂”。但对散户来说，要传达这个理念就难得多。今年我们在私募信贷 BDC 那块就见识到了：所有这些“非上市业务发展公司”（private BDC）从散户那里募资，说“我们把你的钱投进私募信贷，赚一份流动性溢价”。然后关于软件公司出了一些坏消息，所有这些投资者就说“我们想拿回我们的钱”。而那些 BDC 说：“不不不，你们不该这么做。”

turns.en: No, no, we told you only 5% of you are allowed to take them out every quarter.
turns.zh: “不不，我们告诉过你们，每季度只允许 5% 的人赎回。”

turns.en: They were sort of premised on the idea that you wouldn't really want your money back, and then everyone wanted their money back. And there's just a misunderstanding, right? Where the private credit funds are like.
turns.zh: 它们的前提假设是：你其实并不真想要回你的钱。结果人人都想要回钱。这就是一场误会，对吧？那些私募信贷基金的想法是——

turns.en: Is that a liquidity mismatch?
turns.zh: 那是流动性错配（liquidity mismatch）吗？

turns.en: It's not. I don't like that.
turns.zh: 不是。我不喜欢这个说法。

turns.en: It's a psychological liquidity mismatch.
turns.zh: 那是一种“心理上的流动性错配”。

turns.en: Yeah, it's like the retail investors, it turns out, wanted more liquidity than the funds were offering them. And the funds weren't offering them that much liquidity because the funds really were making long-term investments. And it really was a bad idea for them to sell all their long-term investments to meet redemptions. And so you have that problem where it's actually hard to sell illiquid private investments to individual retirement savers. But selling illiquid private investments to retirement savers is both theoretically a good idea because they have long time horizons. They should not care about liquidity. They should be willing to get paid to take some liquidity risk. And it's also just like a good economic proposition for the financial industry because you can't make money giving people public equity exposure and charging them one basis point. So the way to like make money in active management, the way to make money as like an investment manager is to do something in the private's world. And so you see this big push for investment managers to do stuff in the private's world. And the way to do that is to make it look more like a pension. So there's a Wall Street Journal article today, kind of following up on a Bloomberg article from March that I also read about, about basically BlackRock pitching, I don't want to say a pension plan. No, no, no, no.
turns.zh: 对，事实证明，散户想要的流动性比基金能提供的更多。而基金之所以没提供那么多流动性，是因为它们真的在做长期投资，为了满足赎回而卖掉所有长期投资，对它们来说确实是个坏主意。于是你就有了这个难题：把非流动性的私募投资卖给个人退休储蓄者，其实很难。但把非流动性的私募投资卖给退休储蓄者，理论上又是好主意，因为他们时间跨度长，本不该在意流动性，本应愿意为了承担一些流动性风险而收取报酬。而且这对金融行业也是一桩好生意，因为你没法靠“给人公开股票敞口、只收一个基点的费用”来赚钱。所以在主动管理里赚钱的办法、作为投资管理人赚钱的办法，是去私募市场（private markets）里做点事。于是你就看到投资管理人一股脑往私募市场里挤。而做到这一点的办法，就是把它做得更像一个养老金。今天《华尔街日报》有篇文章，算是跟进我此前也读过的一篇 3 月的彭博文章，讲的基本上是贝莱德在推销——我不想说“养老金计划”。不不不不。

turns.en: I want to read to you the exact Wall Street Journal headline. BlackRock plans to make the corporate 401k look more like a pension.
turns.zh: 我想给你念一下《华尔街日报》那个一字不差的标题：“贝莱德计划让企业 401(k) 看起来更像养老金。”

turns.en: Yes.
turns.zh: 对。

turns.en: It's still a 401k, but it looks like a pension.
turns.zh: 它仍然是 401(k)，但看起来像养老金。

turns.en: Yeah. Okay. Right.
turns.zh: 是啊。好。对。

turns.en: It's a pension-like 401k.
turns.zh: 它是一个“类养老金的 401(k)”。

turns.en: Well, what they say is they want to keep the benefits of a 401k, which is portability.
turns.zh: 嗯，他们的说法是：想保留 401(k) 的好处，也就是可携带性（portability）——

turns.en: Yep.
turns.zh: 对。

turns.en: Meaning that you don't have to do that one job forever. And also some amount of individual control with the benefits of the pension, which is professional management and long time horizons. And so what does that mean? I don't know. I'm not sure they know. But my general view is that it means putting private assets into it. I think the main thing that it means conceptually is that instead of telling you the number of dollars in your account, the long-term goal is to tell you the number of dollars you'll get each month in retirement.
turns.zh: ——意思是你不必一辈子只干那一份工作；同时也保留一定程度的个人掌控，再加上养老金的好处，也就是专业管理和长时间跨度。那这到底意味着什么？我不知道，我也不确定他们自己知道。但我大致的看法是，它意味着把私募资产放进去。我觉得从概念上讲，它最主要的意思是：不再告诉你账户里有多少美元，而是把长期目标定为告诉你退休后每月能拿到多少美元。

turns.en: An annuity?
turns.zh: 年金（annuity）？

turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 对。

turns.en: Which is a maybe more practical way to focus your mind on.
turns.zh: 这也许是一种更实际的、能让你把注意力集中上去的方式。

turns.en: Sure, sure. But like the way you implement that in a 401k is like you have some investment account, let's say a target date fund, maybe a target date fund that includes a great heaping helping of private assets. And your target date fund targets your retirement date. And when you hit the retirement date, it switches from a target date fund into an annuity. Like you just use the balance in the target date fund to buy an annuity. And the annuity pays you X thousand dollars a month until you die or for some fixed period of years. That's a pension, right? I mean, that's like to you that has the experience of a pension. Except that you don't know what the number of dollars every month is until you retire because they buy the annuity when you retire. But there are ways around that. You can estimate. You can buy forward starting annuities. You can structure around that if you are a professional asset manager.
turns.zh: 当然，当然。但在 401(k) 里实现这一点的办法是：你有一个投资账户，比如一只目标日期基金，也许是一只包含了“一大勺”私募资产的目标日期基金。你的目标日期基金瞄准你的退休日期，等你到了退休日期，它就从目标日期基金切换成年金——你就是用目标日期基金里的余额去买一份年金。这份年金每月付你 X 千美元，一直付到你去世，或者付满某个固定年限。那就是养老金，对吧？我是说，对你而言那就是养老金的体验。只不过在你退休之前，你不知道每月那个美元数字是多少，因为他们是等你退休时才买年金。但这有办法绕过去：你可以估算，你可以买“远期起息年金”（forward starting annuities）——如果你是个专业资产管理人，你可以围绕它设计结构。

turns.en: I am not.
turns.zh: 我可不是（专业资产管理人）。

turns.en: Right. So, like, I think the idea is, like, this is all baby steps because it's all optional because people have 401ks and some people are used to 401ks and they're like, I just want to own index funds.
turns.zh: 对。所以我觉得这个理念是：这一切都是“婴儿学步”式的小步走，因为它全都是可选的——人们有 401(k)，有些人已经习惯了 401(k)，他们会说“我就想持有指数基金”。

turns.en: Right.
turns.zh: 对。

turns.en: But, like, the idea, I think, would have to be that in a perfect world, a company would offer its employees to push a button and the button is, like, BlackRock will give you X thousand dollars in retirement and, like, that's that. And, like, BlackRock... figures out how to get there.
turns.zh: 但我觉得，这个理念要成立的话，在一个完美的世界里，公司会给员工一个按钮可以按，这个按钮就是：“贝莱德会在你退休时给你 X 千美元，就这么定了。”而贝莱德……去想办法实现它。

turns.en: Right.
turns.zh: 对。

turns.en: And the way they get there is keeping helpings of private assets.
turns.zh: 而他们实现这一点的办法，是往里面加入一份份（大份的）私募资产。

turns.en: Right, right, right.
turns.zh: 对，对，对。

turns.en: And the structure of it is they buy assets and hold them until retirement and then they- It's like.
turns.zh: 它的结构是：他们买入资产，一直持有到退休，然后就——这就像——

turns.en: An elegant way to say don't worry about the short-term kind of stuff. Don't worry about the software stocks in the- Right.
turns.zh: ——一种优雅的说法：“别担心短期那些东西，别担心那些软件股——”对。

turns.en: It's like focusing people's minds away from the dollar balance in their 401k, which went down today because of AI.
turns.zh: 这就像是把人们的注意力，从他们 401(k) 里那个“今天因为 AI 而下跌”的美元余额上引开。

turns.en: Right, right. Yeah, yeah, yeah.
turns.zh: 对，对。是是是。

turns.en: Focus it on, like, you get a long-term pension, don't worry about it.
turns.zh: 把注意力引到：“你会拿到一份长期养老金，别操心它。”

turns.en: Yeah, yeah, yeah. So psychologically a pension.
turns.zh: 是是是。所以，从心理上它就是一份养老金。
